**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5654695, Reactome:R-HSA-5654699, Reactome:R-HSA-5654700, Reactome:R-HSA-5654727, Reactome:R-HSA-5655253)

**Proposed mechanism:** FGFR2 (HGNC:3671) —INCREASES→ FGF signaling pathway; FGF10 (HGNC:3610) —INCREASES→ FGF signaling pathway; FGF signaling pathway —LEADS_TO→ Cutis gyrata (HP:0000981); FGF signaling pathway —DECREASES→ Aplasia/hypoplasia of lacrimal glands (HP:0030181); FGF signaling pathway —DECREASES→ Aplasia/hypoplasia of salivary glands (HP:0030182). Gain-of-function mutations in FGFR2 or FGF10 lead to aberrant activation of the FGF signaling pathway, resulting in phenotypes like cutis gyrata (Beare-Stevenson syndrome). Conversely, loss-of-function mutations in FGFR2 or FGF10 disrupt the normal FGF signaling pathway, leading to developmental defects such as aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands.

**How to falsify it:** If specific loss-of-function variants in FGFR2 or FGF10 are found to cause Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome, or if specific gain-of-function variants in FGFR2 or FGF10 are found to cause aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands, this hypothesis would be falsified.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the opposing roles of FGFR2 and FGF10 in these distinct developmental processes could inform therapeutic strategies targeting the FGF signaling pathway for craniofacial and ectodermal development disorders.
